segments.say: Perhaps, as you've listened tonight, a part of you has been thinking, this all sounds lovely, but I'm an introvert. I like quiet evenings. A busy party leaves me exhausted. Talking to strangers on a train sounds like my idea of a nightmare. Is all this research really about people like me?

show.title: Myth fourteen: introverts don't need connection

segments.say: It's a very fair question. People really do differ in how much social stimulation they enjoy. Extraversion, one of the big personality traits, captures exactly this. Some people gain energy from being around others. Some people find that same energy draining, and need time alone to recharge. Both are completely normal.

In recent years, there's been a welcome wave of appreciation for quieter people, in books, articles and conversations. And that's a good thing. But sometimes it has slipped into a different idea. That introverts simply don't need connection very much, and are happiest left alone. The research tells a more nuanced story.

In 2002, William Fleeson and his colleagues asked people to report, several times a day, how they were behaving and how they felt. How talkative, bold and energetic were you just now? And how happy? They found that in the moments when people were acting in more outgoing ways, they tended to feel more positive. And this was true for introverts as well as extraverts.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2002
show.what: An intraindividual process approach to the relationship between extraversion and positive affect: is acting extraverted as good as being extraverted?

segments.say: That's a striking finding. It suggests that the good feelings that come with social engagement aren't only for extraverts. Introverts, too, often feel better in the moments when they're engaging with others. They may simply need those moments in smaller doses, with more recovery time in between.

In 2012, John Zelenski and his colleagues asked people to act either more outgoing or more reserved during a group discussion. When introverts acted in a more outgoing way, they generally reported feeling more positive, without clear costs to how well they thought. In a follow-up study published in 2013, the same research group found that introverts tended to overestimate how unpleasant acting outgoing would feel.

show.what: Would introverts be better off if they acted more like extraverts? Exploring emotional and cognitive consequences of counterdispositional behavior

segments.say: That fits a theme we've seen throughout tonight. People tend to expect social interactions to be harder and less pleasant than they turn out to be. Introverts may be especially likely to make this prediction. The anticipation of socialising can feel worse than the socialising itself.
But it's important not to swing too far the other way. Acting against your nature isn't free.

In 2017, Sointu Leikas and Ville-Juhani Ilmarinen tracked people's behaviour and feelings over a couple of weeks. In the moments when people acted extraverted, they tended to feel better right then. But a few hours later, they tended to report more tiredness.

show.what: Happy now, tired later? Extraverted and conscientious behavior are related to immediate mood gains, but to later fatigue

segments.say: So both things seem to be true at once. Social engagement often gives a mood boost, even for introverts. And it can also be tiring, leaving people needing rest afterwards. That's not a contradiction. It's a bit like a lovely long walk. It feels good, and afterwards you're glad to sit down.

show.sub: A lift, then a need to rest

segments.say: And that brings us to something that deserves to be said clearly. Time alone isn't a failure of connection. It can be a valuable part of a healthy life.

In 2018, Thuy-vy Nguyen, Richard Ryan and Edward Deci asked people to spend fifteen minutes alone, without phones or other distractions. Afterwards, people tended to feel calmer, with fewer intense emotions, whether positive or negative. Solitude seemed to work as a kind of emotional reset.

show.what: Solitude as an approach to affective self-regulation

segments.say: Importantly, the effects depended partly on why people were alone. Solitude that people chose freely tended to feel more restful than solitude that felt forced on them. Being alone by choice is very different from feeling lonely. One is a quiet room you step into. The other is a door that feels locked.

Loneliness researchers make this point too. Loneliness isn't the same as being alone. It's the painful feeling that our connections are fewer or less close than we need. An introvert with two deep friendships and plenty of quiet evenings may feel far less lonely than an extravert surrounded by people who don't really know them.
So for quieter people, connection may simply look different. Fewer people. Deeper conversations. Long walks with one friend rather than a crowded party.

Remember the research on deep conversations. People enjoyed going deeper more than they expected. That may suit many introverts perfectly. One meaningful conversation might be worth more to them than a dozen light chats. Sitting side by side doing something together, reading, cooking, walking, can be a deep form of connection too, even with few words.

show.title: Connection for quiet people
items: Deeper conversations rather than small talk

segments.say: For many quieter people, it can help to think of social energy a little like a budget for the week. Not something to hoard, but something to spend wisely. Perhaps one evening with friends, then a quiet evening to recover. A long conversation with one person rather than a big gathering. Knowing your own rhythm isn't avoiding connection. It's making room for the kind that nourishes you.

Think of two old friends fishing on a quiet lake, barely speaking for an hour, perfectly content. Or two people reading in the same room on a rainy afternoon. Some of the deepest connections happen in comfortable silence, where nobody has to perform, and simply being together is enough.

So, do introverts need connection? Yes, in their own way. The research suggests that most of us, whatever our personality, feel better for genuine contact with others. But the amount, the setting and the rhythm can be very different. The goal isn't to become someone else. It's to find the kind of connection that fits you, and to give yourself the quiet you need around it.

And perhaps that's one more reason some connections feel so intense even when nothing is said. With the right person, silence stops being awkward and becomes a kind of closeness in itself. You don't have to fill it. You can simply be there, together.

show.sub: Perhaps the most intense of all

segments.say: We've now gone through all fourteen beliefs. In the final chapter, we'll gather together what we've learned about why some connections feel so intense. And then, we'll slow everything right down, into a gentle wind-down for the rest of the evening.
